questions.question: What is the name of the thread on which the JVM calls your main method?
questions.explanation: The JVM starts one thread named main and runs the main method on it.

questions.question: What do the threads of one Java process share?
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own stack, but all threads of a process share objects on the heap.

questions.question: What does this print? Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()), "lane-7"); t.run();
questions.explanation: run() called directly is a plain method call, so the lambda executes on the current thread, main.

questions.question: What goes wrong here? Thread t = new Thread(task); t.start(); t.start();
options: The task runs twice in parallel
The second call is silently ignored
questions.explanation: A thread can be started only once. Create a new Thread object to run the task again.

questions.question: What does this print? Thread t = new Thread(() -> {}); System.out.println(t.getState());
questions.explanation: The thread object exists but start() was never called, so its state is NEW.

questions.question: Why is implementing Runnable usually preferred over extending Thread?
options: Only Runnable can use the run() method
Extending Thread is not allowed after Java 8
The class stays free to extend another class, and the task can go to a thread pool
questions.explanation: Java allows one superclass, and a Runnable task is separate from the thread that runs it.

questions.question: A worker thread fills int[] totals, and main prints totals[0] right after worker.start(). Why can it print 0?
options: main did not call worker.join() before reading
int arrays cannot be shared between threads
totals must be a String array
questions.explanation: Without join(), main may read before the worker finishes. join() waits and makes the worker's writes visible.

questions.question: A thread tries to enter a synchronized block whose lock another thread holds. What is its state?
questions.explanation: Waiting for a monitor lock is the BLOCKED state. WAITING is for join(), wait() and similar calls.

questions.question: What does this print? Thread t = new Thread(() -> {}); t.start(); t.join(); System.out.println(t.getState());
questions.explanation: join() returns only after run() has finished, so the thread is TERMINATED.

questions.question: Which checked exception must you handle or declare when calling join()?
questions.explanation: join() can be interrupted while waiting, so it declares throws InterruptedException.
